title: API Keys, OAuth Scopes, Rate Limits and Quotas
oneLiner: The checks every request passes before your handler runs: who is calling, what they may do, to which object, and how often.
keyTakeaway: Each API request goes through the same gates, in order: authenticate the caller (an API key for server-to-server calls, an OAuth access token when acting for a user), check its rate limits and quotas, check the token's scopes allow this kind of action, and check this caller may touch this particular object. Each failure has its own answer: 401 for no or bad credentials, 403 for a missing scope or permission (or 404 to hide that the object exists), 429 with Retry-After for limits. Rate limits protect the service over seconds; quotas enforce a plan over days or months; both should be visible to clients in response headers.
explanation:
This lesson is an overview of the parts of an API that aren't about any one endpoint. The Security section covers authentication and OAuth in depth, and the Rate Limiting lesson and the Design a Rate Limiter walk-through cover the algorithms; here the question is how they fit into an API design.

Authentication answers "who is calling?". An API key is a long random secret issued to a developer or a service, sent in a header (Authorization: Bearer sk_live_... or X-API-Key) on every request. Keys are simple and suit server-to-server calls, but they identify an application, not a user, and anyone who copies one can use it until it is revoked. Treat them like passwords: store only a hash, show the full key once, use a recognisable prefix (sk_live_, ghp_) so leaked keys can be found by secret scanners, let customers create several keys and rotate them, and never put one in a mobile app or web page, where anyone can extract it.

When a third-party app acts for a user (a scheduling tool reading your calendar), the user should never hand over their password. OAuth 2.0 solves this: the app sends the user to the provider, the user logs in there and approves a list of permissions, and the app receives an access token, a short-lived credential (minutes to an hour) that it sends as Authorization: Bearer <token>, plus a refresh token to get new ones. The authorization code flow with PKCE (now recommended for every app, and essential for mobile and browser apps that can't keep a secret) protects the exchange; for one service calling another with no user, the client credentials grant issues a token to the service itself. Access tokens are often JWTs (signed JSON) that a gateway can verify without calling the auth server, which is fast but means a token can't easily be revoked before it expires, which is one reason they are short-lived.

Authorization answers "may this caller do this?", at two levels. Scopes are the coarse level: the permissions the token was granted, such as photos:read or calendar.events.write. Design them around what users understand when they approve (read versus write, per area of the product), not one per endpoint, and give each token the fewest it needs. A valid token without the needed scope gets 403 with error="insufficient_scope" in the WWW-Authenticate header. The fine level is per object: a token with photos:write may edit the user's own photos, not someone else's. Checking that on every request, in the handler or a shared policy, is the single most important security check in an API: OWASP's API Security Top 10 puts broken object level authorization (BOLA), changing /photos/123 to /photos/124 and getting someone else's photo, at number one. Return 404 rather than 403 when the caller shouldn't learn that the object exists.

Rate limits and quotas answer "how much?". A rate limit caps short-term speed (100 requests per second per key, with bursts allowed by a token bucket) to protect the service from overload and from one customer using up shared capacity. A quota caps total use over a billing period (10,000 calls a day on the free plan, a million on the paid one) and is a product and pricing decision. Limits can be per key, per user, per IP address for anonymous traffic, per endpoint (search and login are usually stricter), and per tenant. Tell clients where they stand: the IETF RateLimit header fields (RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset, or the older X-RateLimit-* versions GitHub uses) on every response, and 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After when they are over. A good client waits that long instead of retrying immediately, which only makes things worse.

Where these checks run: usually in an API gateway, the front-door service every request passes through, which terminates TLS, validates keys and tokens, enforces rate limits and quotas, and records usage for billing before forwarding the request. Object-level authorization can't live there, because only the service knows who owns photo 124, so it stays in the service. Order matters: authenticate first, so an attacker without a key can't use up a real customer's quota, and run the cheap checks before the expensive ones.

The widget sends requests through those gates. Part 1 lets you choose the caller and the request and shows which gate stops it and with what status. Part 2 runs a client against a rate limit with the headers it returns, and compares a client that retries immediately with one that honours Retry-After.
